title: 10 Git Concepts Seniors Use Daily
summary: Ten Git concepts beyond add/commit/push, covering twelve commands: switch, restore, stash, log --graph, blame -w, cherry-pick, worktree, rebase -i, commit --fixup, reflog, bisect and range-diff. Each concept covers what it is, why it exists, a worked example, its trade-offs and the interview takeaway, and the book closes with a cheatsheet.

chapters.title: 10 Git Concepts Seniors Use Daily
points: Cover: 10 concepts that cover 12 commands beyond add/commit/push
The set: switch, restore, stash, log --graph, blame -w, cherry-pick, worktree, rebase -i, commit --fixup, reflog, bisect, range-diff
Ordered from daily-driver basics to history surgery and recovery
Common thread: Git stores snapshots and moves pointers, so most mistakes are recoverable

chapters.title: switch and restore
points: What it is: git switch changes branches; git restore changes files in the working tree or index. Both arrived in Git 2.23 to split the overloaded git checkout
Why it exists: git checkout did two unrelated jobs, so 'git checkout foo' could mean branch foo or file foo, and typos silently discarded work
Used for: switch for moving or creating branches; restore for discarding edits or unstaging

How it works: 'git switch -c fix/login origin/main' creates and moves to a new branch off origin/main. 'git restore src/a.js' discards unstaged edits, 'git restore --staged src/a.js' unstages, 'git restore --source=HEAD~2 src/a.js' pulls the file from two commits ago
Benefits: one verb per intent; restore --staged replaces the cryptic 'reset HEAD file'; switch refuses to clobber a dirty tree; --source reads any commit's version
Consider: 'git restore file' permanently drops uncommitted edits (not in reflog); switch -c needs a start point or it uses HEAD; '--detach' leaves you on a detached HEAD
Interview takeaway: switch moves HEAD, restore rewrites files, and neither rewrites history. 'restore --staged' only unstages, while 'restore' alone destroys unstaged work

chapters.title: stash
points: What it is: git stash shelves uncommitted changes on a stack and returns the tree to a clean HEAD
Why it exists: you need a clean tree to switch branches or pull, but the work is not ready to commit
Used for: urgent hotfix interruptions, pulling with a dirty tree, moving half-done work to another branch

How it works: 'git stash push -m "wip: cart total"' saves tracked changes as stash@{0}. 'git stash list' shows the stack, 'git stash pop' applies the newest and drops it, 'git stash apply stash@{1}' applies and keeps it. Under the hood each stash is a merge commit on refs/stash
Benefits: instant clean tree; -u includes untracked files; -p stashes chosen hunks only; 'git stash branch fix-cart' turns a stash into a branch
Consider: untracked and ignored files are skipped without -u or -a; pop on conflict keeps the stash; stashes are easy to forget, so name them with -m; they are local only and never pushed
Interview takeaway: stash is a stack of temporary commits, not a backup. Prefer apply over pop when unsure, and commit to a WIP branch for anything long-lived

chapters.title: Reading History: log --graph and blame -w
points: What it is: 'git log --graph' draws the commit DAG in ASCII; 'git blame -w' shows who last changed each line while ignoring whitespace-only changes
Why it exists: history is a graph, not a list, and a reformat commit hides the real author of a line
Used for: understanding merges and branch topology; finding why a line exists; tracing code authorship

How it works: 'git log --graph --oneline --decorate --all' draws every branch as a graph with branch labels. 'git blame -w -L 40,60 src/pay.js' blames lines 40-60 skipping whitespace edits. Add -M and -C to follow lines moved or copied across files
Benefits: the graph exposes diverged branches and merge points at a glance; -w stops an indent-only commit from stealing credit; -L limits output to a range

Consider: blame shows the last touch, not the origin, so follow the chain with 'git log -L 40,60:src/pay.js'; for a bulk reformat use --ignore-rev or the .git-blame-ignore-revs file; the graph is unreadable on huge repos without --first-parent
Interview takeaway: blame answers who last changed a line, log -S/-L answers when it appeared. Use -w -M -C to see past cosmetic edits and refactor moves

chapters.title: cherry-pick
points: What it is: git cherry-pick copies the change introduced by a commit onto the current branch as a new commit
Why it exists: sometimes you need one fix without merging the whole branch it lives on
Used for: backporting a hotfix to release/1.4; recovering a commit from an abandoned branch; pulling a single commit from a teammate

How it works: on release/1.4 run 'git cherry-pick a1b2c3d'. Git diffs a1b2c3d against its parent and applies that patch, creating a new commit with a different hash and the same message. Use -x to append '(cherry picked from a1b2c3d)'; use a range 'A^..B' for several commits
Benefits: surgical, with no merge noise; -x leaves an audit trail; -n applies the change without committing; -m 1 can pick a merge commit relative to its first parent
Consider: the copy has a new SHA, so merging both branches later can conflict or duplicate; conflicts resolve with --continue or --abort; picking merges requires -m
Interview takeaway: cherry-pick replays a diff, not a commit. The result is a different commit, so use it for backports and prefer merge or rebase for normal integration

chapters.title: worktree
points: What it is: git worktree adds extra working directories that share one repository's .git object store, each with its own checked-out branch
Why it exists: stash and switch interrupt your flow, and a second clone duplicates the entire history on disk
Used for: reviewing a PR while your work stays untouched; running a long test on one branch while you code on another; parallel agent sessions

How it works: 'git worktree add ../app-hotfix -b hotfix/401 origin/main' creates a folder with a new branch. Work and commit there, then 'git worktree remove ../app-hotfix'. 'git worktree list' shows every tree. Metadata is kept in .git/worktrees/
Benefits: no stashing; shared objects mean cheap disk use and instant fetches; separate build dirs and files per branch

Consider: a branch can be checked out in only one worktree at a time; each tree needs its own node_modules or venv; delete with 'worktree remove' or run 'worktree prune' for stale entries, never just rm -rf
Interview takeaway: worktrees give parallel checkouts from a single repo. Reach for them over stash or a second clone when you need two branches live at once

chapters.title: rebase -i
points: What it is: git rebase -i replays a range of commits onto a base while letting you edit the plan: reorder, squash, reword, edit, drop
Why it exists: the first draft of history is messy ('wip', 'fix typo'), and reviewers want a clean, logical sequence
Used for: squashing WIP commits before a PR; rewording messages; splitting a large commit; dropping debug commits

How it works: 'git rebase -i HEAD~4' opens a todo list with lines like 'pick a1b2c3d add cart', 'pick e4f5a6b wip', 'pick 9c8d7e6 fix typo'. Change the second and third to 'fixup' to fold them into the first, save, and the result is one clean commit. Commands: pick, reword, edit, squash, fixup, drop
Benefits: readable, bisectable history; fixes mistakes before sharing; --onto moves a branch to a new base; --abort restores the original state

Consider: it rewrites SHAs, so never rebase commits others have pulled; after rebasing a pushed branch use 'git push --force-with-lease', never plain --force; conflicts may repeat per commit (rerere helps)
Interview takeaway: rebase -i rewrites history by creating new commits. Use it freely on private branches, never on shared ones, and force-push with --force-with-lease

chapters.title: commit --fixup and autosquash
points: What it is: 'git commit --fixup <sha>' records a commit labeled 'fixup! <original subject>'; 'rebase -i --autosquash' automatically reorders and folds it into its target
Why it exists: you spot a bug in an earlier commit while mid-feature, and manually editing the rebase todo list is slow and error-prone
Used for: applying review feedback to the right commit; keeping a PR as a clean series of logical commits

How it works: after commit 3f2a1bc 'add cart total', fix a rounding bug and run 'git commit --fixup 3f2a1bc'. The new commit is titled 'fixup! add cart total'. Then 'git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main' moves it directly under 3f2a1bc and marks it fixup, so you only save and exit
Benefits: no manual todo editing; 'git config rebase.autoSquash true' makes it the default; --squash! variant also lets you edit the message; 'git commit --fixup=amend:<sha>' rewrites the message
Consider: the target must be in the rebase range; it still rewrites history, with the same shared-branch rule as rebase -i; find the sha with 'git log --oneline' or 'git absorb'
Interview takeaway: fixup commits are a marker plus autosquash, a way to correct an old commit without opening the todo list. Set rebase.autoSquash to true

chapters.title: reflog
points: What it is: git reflog is a local log of every position HEAD and each branch tip has had, including resets, rebases and checkouts
Why it exists: commits that are no longer reachable from any branch look lost, but Git still holds them for a while
Used for: undoing a bad reset --hard or rebase; recovering a deleted branch; finding where HEAD was yesterday

How it works: after an accidental 'git reset --hard HEAD~3', run 'git reflog' and find 'e4f5a6b HEAD@{1}: commit: add cart'. Then 'git reset --hard e4f5a6b' or 'git branch rescue e4f5a6b' brings it back. Use main@{2.days.ago} for time-based lookups
Benefits: a safety net for nearly every history mistake; per-branch logs; works with any ref syntax such as HEAD@{n}
Consider: local only, not pushed or cloned; entries expire after 90 days (30 for unreachable) before gc prunes them; uncommitted changes were never recorded, so they cannot be recovered
Interview takeaway: reflog is the undo history for refs. 'Committed once' means recoverable, 'never committed' means gone

chapters.title: bisect
points: What it is: git bisect binary-searches your commit history to find the exact commit that introduced a bug
Why it exists: when a regression appears across hundreds of commits, checking each one by hand is slow
Used for: pinpointing a regression; automating the hunt with a test script

How it works: run 'git bisect start', 'git bisect bad' (current HEAD is broken), 'git bisect good v2.3' (known working tag). With 128 commits in between, Git checks out the midpoint and you mark good or bad, and about 7 steps (log2 128) isolate the culprit. Finish with 'git bisect reset'
Benefits: O(log n) steps; 'git bisect run npm test' automates it fully; skip untestable commits with 'git bisect skip'; bisect log can be replayed
Consider: needs a reliable good/bad test; exit code 125 tells run to skip; the good commit must be a true ancestor; merge-heavy history gives fuzzy culprits, so use --first-parent
Interview takeaway: bisect finds the first bad commit in log2(n) steps, and 'bisect run' with a script makes it hands-free. Small, atomic commits make it exact

chapters.title: range-diff
points: What it is: git range-diff compares two versions of a commit series, such as a PR before and after a rebase, commit by commit
Why it exists: after a force-push, a plain diff mixes your real changes with the upstream rebase noise, so reviewers can't tell what changed
Used for: reviewing a v2 of a patch series; verifying that a rebase or conflict resolution changed nothing unintended

How it works: 'git range-diff main old-branch new-branch' pairs commits by patch similarity and prints markers: '=' unchanged, '!' modified (with an inner diff), '<' dropped, '>' added. Shorthand: 'git range-diff @{u}...@' or 'git range-diff A...B'
Benefits: it diffs the diff, so only real changes appear; it finds reordered or squashed commits; it works after force-push using the reflog's old tip
Consider: you need the old tip (a saved branch, the reflog or @{u}); heavily rewritten commits may fail to pair and show as drop+add; output is dense and best read in a pager
Interview takeaway: range-diff compares patch series, not trees. Use it to review a force-pushed PR without re-reading everything, and keep the old tip reachable

chapters.title: Git Commands Cheatsheet
points: Switch branch: git switch -c name origin/main
Discard or unstage: git restore f | git restore --staged f | git restore --source=HEAD~2 f
Shelve work: git stash push -m msg -u | git stash apply | git stash pop
Read history: git log --graph --oneline --decorate --all | git blame -w -M -C -L 40,60 f
Backport: git cherry-pick -x sha | git cherry-pick A^..B
Parallel checkout: git worktree add ../dir -b name | git worktree remove ../dir
Clean up history: git rebase -i HEAD~4 | git commit --fixup sha | git rebase -i --autosquash main | git push --force-with-lease
Recover and debug: git reflog | git reset --hard HEAD@{1} | git bisect start/bad/good/run | git range-diff main old new
